title: Load balancers: layers, algorithms, health
summary: L4 and L7 load balancers, reverse proxies and TLS termination; round robin, smooth weighted round robin, least connections, power of two choices and ring hashing; active and passive health checks and connection draining.

steps.title: L4 or L7
body: A load balancer spreads requests over a pool of servers and stops sending to the ones that are sick.
The big choice is which layer it understands.
| | L4 (transport: TCP/UDP) | L7 (application: HTTP, gRPC) |
| Sees | addresses, ports, connections | methods, paths, headers, cookies |
| Balances | connections | individual requests (many per connection with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) |
| Can do | pass TLS through untouched, any protocol, millions of connections cheaply | route `/api` vs `/static`, canaries by header, retries, TLS termination, compression |
| Costs | little CPU, almost no added latency | parses every request; a little more latency and CPU |
- **Reverse proxy**: a server that accepts client requests and forwards them to backends (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy). An L7 load balancer is a reverse proxy with a pool.
- **TLS termination**: the proxy decrypts TLS so it can read HTTP; it may re-encrypt to the backends.
- **API gateway**: an L7 proxy with API concerns on top: authentication, scopes, rate limits, versions. The *Integration* topic covers it in depth.
A classic trap: an L4 balancer with HTTP/2 or gRPC. One long-lived connection carries every request from a
client, so one backend gets all of it while others sit idle. Balance gRPC at L7 (per request).

steps.prompt: Which layer do you need for each requirement?
items: Send `/images/*` to one pool and `/api/*` to another
Spread PostgreSQL connections over read replicas
Send requests with header `X-Canary: 1` to the new version
Keep TLS end to end without the balancer seeing the content
Retry an idempotent GET on another server after a 503
Spread gRPC calls from one client over many backends
steps.explain: Anything that looks inside a request (paths, headers, status codes) or balances individual requests on a shared connection needs L7. Plain connection spreading and TLS pass-through are L4 jobs.

steps.title: Algorithms
body: | Algorithm | How it picks | Good for | Weakness |
| Round robin | next server in turn | identical servers, similar requests | ignores a slow or busy server |
| Weighted round robin | in turn, in proportion to weights | mixed server sizes, canaries | still blind to load |
| Least connections / least outstanding requests | the server with the fewest in flight | uneven request costs, a slow server | needs the balancer to track counts |
| Power of two random choices | pick two at random, take the less loaded | many balancers with stale load info | slightly less exact than full least-loaded |
| Ring hash / Maglev (consistent hashing) | hash a key (user, session) to a server | cache affinity, sticky sessions | hot keys; uneven load |
**Smooth weighted round robin** (the algorithm nginx uses) avoids bursts. With weights a=5, b=1, c=1 a naive
version sends `aaaaabc`; the smooth one interleaves `aabacaa`. Each round, every server's *current* value grows
by its weight, the biggest wins, and the winner pays back the total weight. Step through it:

steps.prompt: Smooth weighted round robin with weights a=3, b=1 (ties go to the first server). What does this print?
steps.explain: Currents go (3,1) -> a wins, (-1,1); (2,2) tie -> a, (-2,2); (1,3) -> b, (1,-1); (4,0) -> a, (0,0). Three a's and one b, with the b in the middle instead of at the end.

steps.title: Health checks and draining
body: - **Active health check**: the balancer calls `/healthz` every few seconds. A server is marked down after `fall` failures in a row and up again after `rise` successes in a row, so one blip does not flap it.

- **Passive health check (outlier detection)**: the balancer watches real traffic and ejects a server that returns too many 5xx or times out, for a while. It reacts to real failures, including a server that answers `/healthz` fine but fails real work.

- **Readiness vs liveness**: *ready* means "send me traffic" (dependencies reachable, warmed up); *live* means "do not restart me". A health endpoint that checks the database makes every server fail at once when the database blips: keep the load-balancer check shallow, and let outlier detection catch real errors.
- **Connection draining**: when a server is removed (deploy, scale-in), stop sending new requests and let in-flight ones finish within a timeout. Without it every deploy drops requests.
Health checks only help if the pool has room left: losing 1 of 4 servers moves 33% more load onto each of the other three.

prompt: **Dashboard snapshot.** A pool of 10 identical servers behind round robin. Overall p99 rose from 120 ms to 900 ms.
Per-server panels: nine servers show p99 around 110 ms; `app-07` shows p99 of 2.4 s and long garbage-collection
pauses, but its `/healthz` answers 200. What change on the balancer helps most right now?
options: Switch to least outstanding requests and turn on outlier detection, so slow app-07 gets less traffic or is ejected
Lower the active health-check interval from 5 s to 1 s
Switch to ring hash so each user always lands on the same server
Add five more servers to the pool
explain: Round robin keeps sending app-07 10% of requests, and those make the p99. Least-outstanding sends work where
it finishes, and outlier detection ejects a server whose real requests fail or crawl. The health check passes,
so checking it faster changes nothing. More servers dilute the problem but app-07 still serves its share.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: the edge, measured
steps.body: When a request is slow or lands on the wrong server, measure each hop yourself before changing anything.

toolkit.what: Shows what DNS really answers, with the remaining TTL in the second column.
flags: just the answer section, with TTLs
toolkit.when: checking a DNS failover or a TTL change

toolkit.what: Splits one request into DNS, TCP connect, TLS, time to first byte and total.
flags: drop the body, no progress bar
toolkit.example: curl -s -o /dev/null -w 'dns %{time_namelookup} tcp %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n' https://shop.example.com/

toolkit.what: Shows whether a response is cacheable and was served from cache: `Cache-Control`, `Age` (seconds in cache) and vendor headers such as `X-Cache`.
flags: ask for the same variant a browser would

toolkit.what: nginx's pool definition: algorithm, weights and passive health checks (open-source nginx has no active checks; those are an NGINX Plus feature).
flags: pick the server with the fewest active connections
after 3 failures, skip the server for 10 s
toolkit.example: upstream api { least_conn; server 10.0.1.11:8080 weight=5 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s; server 10.0.1.12:8080; }

toolkit.what: HAProxy's pool with active health checks and rise/fall thresholds.
flags: check every 2 s; up after 2 passes, down after 3 failures
toolkit.example:
backend api
  balance leastconn
  option httpchk GET /healthz
  server app1 10.0.1.11:8080 check inter 2s rise 2 fall 3

toolkit.what: A load generator that sends a **constant rate** and records latency without coordinated omission (it does not slow down when the server does).
flags: print the full latency percentile table
toolkit.when: finding a server's knee: rerun at rising -R

toolkit.what: Scripted load tests in JavaScript; the `constant-arrival-rate` executor keeps the request rate fixed like wrk2.
flags: fixed requests per second in the script's options

steps.prompt: Match each option to what it does.
pairs: Up after 2 passing checks, down after 3 failing ones
Skip a server for 10 s after 3 failed requests
Send a constant 2,000 requests per second
Time until the first byte of the response
Only the answer records, with their remaining TTL

steps.prompt: An HAProxy backend that sends each request to the server with the fewest connections, checks `/healthz` every 2 s, and marks a server up after 2 passes and down after 3 failures.
steps.explain: `leastconn` adapts to slow servers; `rise`/`fall` stop a single slow check from flapping the server in and out.

steps.title: Smooth weighted round robin with health
prompt: - `SmoothWrr(string[] names, int[] weights)`: the pool, every server healthy, every *current* value 0.
- `void SetHealthy(string name, bool healthy)`: an unknown name throws `ArgumentException`.
- `string Next()`: for each **healthy** server in order, add its weight to its current value; the healthy server
with the largest current value wins (ties go to the earlier one); subtract the **sum of the healthy weights** from
the winner's current value; return its name. Unhealthy servers keep their current value unchanged. If no
Weights 5, 1, 1 give `aabacaa`; with `b` unhealthy they give `aaacaa`.
starter: public void SetHealthy(string name, bool healthy) { }
solution: public void SetHealthy(string name, bool healthy)
if (i < 0) throw new ArgumentException($"unknown server '{name}'", nameof(name));
if (best < 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("no healthy server");
hints: Keep four arrays: names, weights, current values and a healthy flag. `Array.IndexOf` finds a name.
In `Next`, skip unhealthy servers, sum the healthy weights as you go, and track the index of the largest current value with a strict `>` so ties stay with the earlier server.
template: string dojoRun(SmoothWrr w, int n) { var s = ""; for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) s += w.Next(); return s; }
Dojo.Eq("the pattern repeats", "aabacaaaabacaa", dojoRun(new SmoothWrr(new[] { "a", "b", "c" }, new[] { 5, 1, 1 }), 14));
Dojo.Eq("equal weights alternate", "abab", dojoRun(new SmoothWrr(new[] { "a", "b" }, new[] { 1, 1 }), 4));
Dojo.Eq("an unhealthy server gets nothing", "aaacaa", dojoRun(dojoSick, 6));
Dojo.Eq("a recovered server is back in the rotation", "aabacaa", dojoRun(dojoBack, 7));
